name: Dominion theology
summary: Dominion theology holds that God gave humankind, and through Christ his people, dominion over every area of life, so that Christians should bring family, church, state and economy under biblical law. In its Reconstructionist core (Rushdoony, Bahnsen, North) it expects this to come gradually, through conversion and a voluntary Christian majority, with a limited, decentralized state, strong private property and welfare left to families and churches. Charismatic and Pentecostal forms, notably the New Apostolic Reformation's seven mountains mandate, took up the dominion mandate in a softer form and aim at Christian control of government and culture.
scope: The Reconstructionist core of the movement as set out in Gary North's Liberating Planet Earth (1987) and in Macneil's and Saiya's scholarly accounts of Rushdoony, North and the charismatic dominionists. Where those scholars show the charismatic strand departing from the theocratic elements (death-penalty punishments and the like), the answer is a split. Answers on economics, family and church-state rest on the Reconstructionist texts, since the charismatic sources record no position on them. Catholic integralism and Stephen Wolfe's Calvinist nationalism are excluded.

sources.title: The varieties of American Christian nationalism
sources.author: Nilay Saiya, Politics and Religion
sources.usedFor: The definition of dominionism, the seven mountains mandate and spiritual warfare of charismatic dominionism, and the reconstructionist penal and franchise proposals.

abortion-legal.rationale: Macneil records Rushdoony condemning Roe v. Wade as humanist judicial overreach and North welcoming picketing of clinics legalized by the Supreme Court but 'not by God's Supreme Court'.

armed-group-creates-revolution.rationale: North says the Israelites did not use armed revolution and that Christians must not aid Marxist revolutionary programs (chapter 4 summary).

avoid-deficit-stimulus.rationale: North lists Keynesianism among the envy-driven doctrines and says state debt destroys taxpayers' independent futures (chapters 6 and 9).

basic-income.rationale: North cites 'if anyone will not work, neither shall he eat' and treats state wealth transfers as legislated covetousness, which rules out an unconditional state income (chapters 7 and 8).

central-planning.rationale: North treats central management of all of life as Satan's version of the civil covenant and says politicians cannot plan an entire economy (chapters 8 and 9).

charity-over-state-aid.rationale: In chapters 6 and 7 the family is the primary welfare agency and the church the secondary one, and voluntary biblical institutions are to replace the state's 'pseudo-compassion'.

class-struggle-history.rationale: North calls the Marxist theory that progress comes through class struggle and revolutionary violence 'an evil theory' and says the war is ethical, not a class war (chapter 8 summary).

clerical-rule.rationale: North separates the ministry of the sword from the ministry of the sacraments and has churches only advise other institutions, not compel them (chapter 7; Blueprints appendix).

collective-farming.rationale: North holds private property basic to dominion and condemns state ownership and confiscation of property (chapter 9).

conscription.rationale: North cites Samuel's warning that a human king will draft sons as a mark of the burdens of statism (chapter 8).

consent-of-governed.rationale: North says reconstruction depends on a majority voluntarily accepting the blueprint, yet he locates authority in God rather than in the people (Blueprints appendix, 'Majority Rule').

corporatist-bargaining.rationale: North condemns the 'corporate state', a union of state and business in a planned economy, as fascism and welfare statism (chapter 9).

death-penalty.rationale: North defends the biblical death penalty as something God requires and tells Christians not to flinch at it, and Saiya reports reconstructionists would execute for adultery, witchcraft and blasphemy.

decent-living-guarantee.rationale: North calls state welfare programs legislated covetousness that make families dependent on a failing state and wants voluntary biblical institutions to replace them (chapters 6 and 8).

decide-locally.rationale: North's goal is covenantal civil law 'from local government to a highly limited central government', built from the bottom up with decentralized courts (chapter 8 summary).

defeat-communism.rationale: North says there can be no peace treaty between Christianity and Marxism and hopes conversion reverses Marxism's spread (introduction; chapter 5).

democracy-best.rationale: North says voters who can vote away others' property turn a society socialist, and that democracy is safe only when voters obey God's law (chapter 9).

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: North lists Marxist transformation by revolution, tyranny, social engineering and re-education as the opposite of dominion (chapter 5 summary).

distribute-by-need.rationale: North ties wealth to hard and honest work and poverty to laziness, and treats coercive redistribution as covetousness (chapter 9).

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: North's civil covenant has Moses represent the people before God and not to the people, and Macneil's Rushdoony makes the state an agency, not a source, of law.

economic-freedom.rationale: North says the power to redistribute wealth under central planning eventually destroys human freedom (chapter 8).

equal-outcomes.rationale: North's chapter 9 summary says outright that the equality of wealth is a satanic goal and that wealth flows to those who work hard and honestly.

filial-duty.rationale: North tells adult children to honor parents financially and spiritually, with responsibility shifting to children as parents age (chapter 6 summary).

gradual-change.rationale: North says dominion religion preaches steady transformation, in contrast to the rapid change and revolution of the power religion (chapter 5 summary).

harm-principle.rationale: Saiya reports reconstructionists want civil law punishing adultery, witchcraft and blasphemy, offences that do not harm other people.

land-redistribution.rationale: North reads the Naboth story as a warning against using the state to take property, and calls redistribution by majority vote theft (chapter 8).

laws-from-scripture.rationale: North writes that 'what we can and should strive for is to conform our human law codes to the explicit requirements of the Ten Commandments and the case-law applications of Biblical law' (chapter 8).

limit-growth.rationale: North treats compound economic growth and handed-down capital as blessings to be multiplied, with no limit for environmental reasons (chapters 6 and 9).

limit-population.rationale: North's chapter 6 summary calls a growing population a tool of dominion: 'be fruitful and multiply'.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: North says politicians are not competent to plan an economy, calls central planners' claim to omniscience economically fatal, and credits the free market with the greatest upward mobility (chapters 8 and 9).

means-match-ends.rationale: North says Christian society must be built from the bottom up by conversion and self-government, and that a top-down imposition on an unconverted society fails (chapter 8 and the Blueprints appendix).

more-religion-public.rationale: North teaches that the kingdom of God includes every human institution and that Christians must take dominion through all of them, and Saiya defines dominionism as Christian domination of politics and culture.

night-watchman-state.rationale: Macneil reports Rushdoony limiting the state's legitimate sphere to a narrow judicial one, with welfare and education left to families and churches.

no-business-privileges.rationale: North says businesses must not petition the state for tariffs, quotas or below-market loans, as that builds the 'corporate state' (chapter 9).

one-party-rule.rationale: In North's account of Satan's civil covenant the ruler represents the Party or the Volk and rules top-down, the opposite of his bottom-up appeals-court model (chapter 8).

politics-spiritual-struggle.rationale: North opens his book as 'a war between Satan and God' fought over which law is obeyed, and Saiya reports the charismatic strand fighting 'territorial spirits' that rule governments.

population-causes-poverty.rationale: North ties lasting poverty to a rebellious society and to laziness, and treats population growth as a blessing (chapters 6 and 9).

profit-exploitation.rationale: North answers the Marxist liberation theologians' attack on the free market by arguing that wealth flows to those who work hard and honestly (chapter 9).

promulgated-standing-laws.rationale: North prizes regular, predictable justice under fixed biblical law and condemns the state's myriad constantly rewritten laws (chapter 8).

property-franchise.rationale: North sets out Ireton's property qualification for the vote as crucial to preserving a democratic order, but he does not make it his own programme (chapter 9).

property-fundamental.rationale: North's chapter on the economy makes private property basic to dominion: the eighth commandment forbids theft, and the civil government is 'to protect private property, not steal it'.

public-ownership.rationale: North calls ownership of property by the state the 'new theology' of modern man and says private property is a cornerstone of civilization (chapter 9 summary).

punish-blasphemy.rationale: Saiya reports reconstructionists would punish blasphemy and the spread of other religions, while Macneil shows Wagner's charismatic strand distancing itself from the theocratic elements.

reinterpret-religion.rationale: North treats biblical law as God's unchanging principles for all of life, to be applied rather than revised (Blueprints appendix).

religion-illusion.rationale: North quotes Marx on religion and answers that Christianity and Marxism are rival religions at war, with biblical faith the basis of real liberation (introduction).

religions-one-truth.rationale: North teaches no pluralism of law or morality, and calls ultimate pluralism polytheistic or humanistic (Blueprints appendix).

religious-equal-recognition.rationale: North teaches one comprehensive biblical law for every institution and no pluralism of law structures (Blueprints appendix).

religious-offensive-war.rationale: North says Christians fight with weapons that are 'not carnal', and that dominion comes through evangelism and voluntary conversion (chapter 2; Blueprints appendix).

results-over-ideology.rationale: North says the battle is between rival law systems with no neutrality, so policy is judged by biblical law and not by results (chapter 3; Blueprints appendix).

sacred-ruler.rationale: North says a civil ruler represents the people only before God, and that a state raising itself to the place of a god is demonic (chapter 8).

same-sex-marriage.rationale: Saiya reports reconstructionists decry homosexuality and want civil law to follow the Bible, which leaves no room for legal same-sex marriage.

scripture-inerrant.rationale: North says every record, law and judgment in the Bible is God's own word that no Christian should flinch at, and that the Old Testament is not discarded (Blueprints appendix).

separate-church-state.rationale: North and Rushdoony keep church and state as separate jurisdictions, with religious liberty as freedom from state control, yet civil law must follow biblical law and no ground is neutral (chapter 7; Macneil 4.3).

shared-marital-authority.rationale: North states that in the family there is a hierarchy of husbands over wives and cites the husband as head of the wife (chapter 6).

socialized-care.rationale: North says the state 'kidnaps' children through schooling and replaces family care of the young and old, and urges families to resume those duties (chapter 6).

sovereign-above-law.rationale: North writes that the civil government is to be restrained by biblical law (chapter 8).

state-directs-investment.rationale: North condemns state economic assistance and protection for industry as the 'corporate state', a form of welfare state, and says politicians cannot plan an economy (chapter 9).

state-harmful.rationale: North describes the civil government as a God-ordained protector and judge; his target is the 'messianic state', not the state's existence (chapter 8).

state-promotes-atheism.rationale: North says there is no neutral ground and treats the humanist state's schooling as a rival religion that Christians must oppose (chapters 6 and 8).

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: North calls the church a separate jurisdiction that the state must not hamper, tax or control (chapter 7).

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: North names tariffs and import quotas among the state favors that businesses must not petition for, since doing so violates property rights (chapter 9).

tax-inheritance.rationale: North complains that the state taxes away families' inheritance and argues that handing capital down across generations is a biblical duty (chapter 6).

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: North holds the state is not entitled even to a ten percent tithe and calls redistribution by majority vote theft, so higher taxes on the wealthy to fund it contradict his position (chapters 8 and 9).

taxation-theft.rationale: North calls the modern state a thief and says a state taking a tithe or more is ungodly, but he does not condemn every civil tax, so the answer is mixed (chapters 8 and 9).

total-state.rationale: Macneil quotes Rushdoony saying a state claiming jurisdiction 'from cradle to grave' claims to be God, and he assigns church, family and state separate spheres.

traditional-family.rationale: North makes the family the central institution of dominion, with its own covenant, primary welfare role and responsibility for children's education (chapter 6).

universal-healthcare.rationale: North lists state-provided health care for the aged among the family functions the modern state has usurped, and assigns that care to families and churches (chapter 6).

vanguard-party.rationale: North contrasts the Christian inside-out change with the Marxist imposition of change by a top-down revolutionary cadre (chapter 5 summary).

work-for-welfare.rationale: North cites 2 Thessalonians 3:10 so that church charity does not create permanent dependence, though he rejects state welfare itself (chapter 7).

missingStatements.text: Parents, not the state, should have primary responsibility for educating children.
missingStatements.rationale: North makes the family the primary educator and calls the tax-supported public school system a state seizure of family capital, urging parents to withdraw their children.

missingStatements.text: Churches should be exempt from taxation by the state.
missingStatements.rationale: North says the church is a separate jurisdiction and 'tax-immune in God's eyes', and that taxing it violates its immunity.

notes: Strands differ: the charismatic and Pentecostal strand is documented here only on the dominion mandate, government control and spiritual warfare, so its positions on economics, family and law enforcement are not recorded. Rushdoony and North reject a clerical state and say comprehensive legal reform needs a voluntary majority, while Saiya reports reconstructionist proposals for death penalties and a Christian franchise from other texts not opened here. Themes searched in North: law, state, economy, family, church, education, welfare, tax, war and revolution; no usable passages were found on immigration, foreign policy, the environment or technology.
